questions.topic: Domestic sources of the second Red Scare
questions.learningObjective: Explain the domestic causes of the second Red Scare.
questions.stem: Rain stopped the inspection, so I wrote about why Americans turned inward on themselves in the late 1940s. Explain which domestic developments produced the second Red Scare.

answer.exemplar: The second Red Scare grew from American conditions rather than foreign orders: wartime labour and union struggles that business leaders read as communist infiltration, the assassination attempt on a foreign diplomat in California, the Chambers case and its pumpkin papers, the fear of subversion shared by both parties, and the Korean War, which made Soviet aggression seem imminent. Congress, state governments and private employers all had reasons to investigate, so the panic was driven by domestic political and economic anxieties as much as by Soviet actions.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the student can name domestic economic, political and cultural causes of the second Red Scare. Answers citing only Soviet actions or only labour unrest miss the combination.
questions.hint: Look for causes that came from inside the country.

answer.exemplar: A hearing gave investigators a public stage on which accused people had to respond, and refusal to answer could be punished as contempt. questions.learningObjective: Explain the global commitment implied by the doctrine's general language.
questions.stem: A 1949 diary I read had me thinking about how a doctrine hardens into a habit. Since the Truman Doctrine was framed in global terms, what did it oblige the United States to do in Asia and Europe?

options.text: That the United States accepted a responsibility to support free peoples wherever they faced subjugation
That the United States would intervene only in Europe, since Greece and Turkey were the whole policy
options.misconception: Believes the doctrine was limited to Europe

options.text: That other nations had no duty to defend themselves without American instruction
options.misconception: Believes allies had no right to act alone

options.text: That the doctrine applied to domestic political disputes within the United States
options.misconception: Believes the doctrine reached into domestic politics

questions.explanation: By stating a general principle about free peoples resisting subjugation, the doctrine committed the country to a global posture, and Asian commitments followed that logic. The distractors narrow it to Europe, absolve allies or turn it inward.
questions.hint: Consider whether the promise was written broadly or narrowly.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the Berlin blockade revealed about the limits of containment.
questions.stem: A researcher from the agricultural college wanted samples, and we talked about keeping things in place. Explain what the Berlin blockade revealed about the limits of containment in 1948.

answer.exemplar: Containment was designed to stop Soviet expansion, and the blockade showed that it could not easily stop Soviet pressure on a Western position close to the Soviet zone. The Soviet move did not enlarge Soviet control; it tightened the grip on West Berlin and on access to it. Because the Western response had to be limited to a supply operation, the crisis exposed how far the policy of resisting change could be carried without confronting the Soviet Union directly.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the student understands that a defensive policy could not answer every Soviet move near the Soviet zone. Answers claiming the blockade expanded Soviet control contradict the purpose of containment.
questions.hint: Ask whether Soviet actions enlarged or tightened control.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what registration changed for ordinary party members.
questions.stem: Our local association met in the church hall and a retired member spoke about old membership cards. What did registration demand change for ordinary party members beyond the risk of prosecution?

options.text: It turned membership into a recorded fact that employers, associations and the government could check
It required every member to carry the card whenever they voted, as proof of eligibility
options.misconception: Believes members had to show registration cards to vote

options.text: It obliged party members to report their own activities to the justice department each year
options.misconception: Believes members had to report activities annually

options.text: It transferred control of the party's candidate lists to federal examiners
options.misconception: Believes examiners controlled party candidate lists

questions.explanation: Registration created a paper record that employers and officials could request and quote, so a registered name travelled further than the member. The distractors invent voting requirements, reporting duties and examiner control of nominations.
questions.hint: Consider what a card in a government file lets others do.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Hearings as a source of leverage
questions.learningObjective: Explain why investigators focused on association and acquaintance.
questions.stem: A retired member asked why investigators cared about who knew whom. Why did the committees place such emphasis on association and acquaintance rather than only on documented acts?

options.text: Association implied access and influence, so proximity to suspects became itself a sign of risk
Because the constitution required committees to prove membership through personal acquaintance
options.misconception: Believes the constitution set the standard of proof by acquaintance

options.text: Because courts had already ruled that guilt could be proved by association alone
options.misconception: Believes courts accepted association as sufficient proof

options.text: Because witnesses had difficulty remembering the names of people they had never met
options.misconception: Believes witnesses could not remember unfamiliar names

questions.explanation: Investigators treated knowing a suspect as evidence of possible access and influence, widening the circle of people questioned beyond actual participants. The distractors invent a constitutional standard, a court ruling or a memory excuse.
questions.hint: Consider what association was taken to prove.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Synthesize the channels through which information about suspected members circulated.
questions.stem: A bee hotel went up beside the hedge, and I thought about small structures that attract. Which combination best describes how information about suspected party members circulated in the 1950s?

options.text: Through public hearings, private groups and informal files, so unverified names reached employers
Through official channels only, so employers learned of names solely from government notices
options.misconception: Believes official channels were the only route of information

options.text: Through the press alone, since newspapers were the sole publishers of witness testimony
options.misconception: Believes newspapers were the only publishers of testimony

options.text: Through party members themselves, who reported colleagues to the committees in confidence
options.misconception: Believes only party members reported to the committees

questions.explanation: Information travelled through hearings, private compilations and informal files, so unverified names reached employers without passing any official test. The distractors invent a single official channel, a press monopoly or reliance only on party members.
questions.hint: Think about every place a name could be written down.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Domestic sources of the second Red Scare
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the Red Scare cut across party lines.
questions.stem: The federation's annual meeting debated a resolution. Why did the Red Scare cut across party lines in the United States?

options.text: Because anticommunist politics could be used by either party to attack opponents and win votes
Because both parties had identical programmes on defence and on the economy in the 1950s
options.misconception: Believes the two parties had identical programmes in the 1950s

options.text: Because the issue arose only from labour unions, which did not belong to either party
options.misconception: Believes unions rather than politicians drove the issue

options.text: Because voters no longer cared about party labels by the end of the decade
options.misconception: Believes voters had abandoned party loyalty by 1959

questions.explanation: Because anticommunist accusation was usable by either side against its opponents, the issue became a general election asset, and both parties had reason to exploit it. The distractors erase the parties or deny their programmes.
questions.hint: Consider which side benefits from naming a rival's supporter.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how defence contracts sustained communities after a war ended.
questions.stem: The hive sat empty at the end of the season, and I wrote about what remains when the bees leave. Explain why defence contracts could sustain communities long after a war ended.

answer.exemplar: A defence plant offered steady employment, training and demand for housing, transport and services that private investment alone would not have provided in a small town. When the contract was renewed year after year, that activity became the town's economic identity, and the politicians who governed it had a strong reason to protect the appropriation. Even when production fell, the specialised labour force and the suppliers around it kept the region dependent on defence work for decades.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the student explains how a government contract becomes a lasting regional economy. Answers that treat the effect as one year's spending miss the durable structure of jobs and suppliers.
questions.hint: Think about what a plant leaves behind when orders fall.
